# 122 · A cache expiry in milliseconds left expires entries in their last millisecond, found by the relation

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✗ Violation: counterexample found** | functional | low | refactor, behaviour change not intended | [`Expiry#remainingMillis`](../../examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/cache/Expiry.java) | [B9: Regression verification](../../lib/README.md) |

> The same rewrite as example 123, the expire-after-write boolean turned into the time an entry has left, but in milliseconds, as the cache's metrics report it; callers test `<= 0`. The developer states the relation to the previous version, `previous == (result <= 0)`, and the proof finds an entry with a fraction of a millisecond to go: not expired before, no millisecond left now, so expired. The integer division rounds the last fraction of a millisecond down to none.

Tags: [caching](../README.md#tag-caching), [clocks-and-time](../README.md#tag-clocks-and-time), [rounding](../README.md#tag-rounding), [signature-change](../README.md#tag-signature-change)

## The change

Replace `isExpired(writtenAtNanos, ttlNanos, nowNanos)` with `remainingMillis(writtenAtNanos, ttlNanos, nowNanos)`: the time to live less the time since the write, divided by a million, `FOREVER` for an entry that never expires, so that an entry is expired exactly when the result is zero or negative. The four tests and the law in the properties file are rewritten for the milliseconds left; the API contract records the new signature.

The developer declares which inputs the change is meant to affect: `!(writtenAtNanos >= 0 && nowNanos >= writtenAtNanos && ttlNanos > 0)`. The verifier proves that every other input behaves as before, or shows one that does not.

The method's signature changed, so the developer states how the previous version is called from the new parameters: `net.terminalvalue.crosscut.cache.Expiry#isExpired()`. The verifier proves that on every input, the new method agrees with the previous one called that way, or shows one on which it does not.

The result changed its type or its meaning, so the developer states how the two results are related, `previous` being the result of `net.terminalvalue.crosscut.cache.Expiry#isExpired` and `result` the new method's: `previous == (result <= 0)`. The verifier proves that the relation holds on every input where both versions return, and that they throw alike where they throw, or shows an input on which they do not.

**Before** ([`Expiry.java`](../../examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/cache/Expiry.java), line 1):

```java
package net.terminalvalue.crosscut.cache;

/**
 * The expire-after-write test of a cache entry, with {@code Long.MAX_VALUE} as the time to live meaning "never", as
 * Caffeine and Spring's cache abstraction treat it. The clock reading is passed in, so that the cache can be
 * driven by a {@code Clock} in tests and by {@code System.nanoTime()} in production.
 */
    // ...

    public static final long FOREVER = Long.MAX_VALUE;

    /** Whether an entry written at {@code writtenAtNanos} with the given time to live has expired at {@code nowNanos}. */
    public static boolean isExpired(long writtenAtNanos, long ttlNanos, long nowNanos) {
        if (ttlNanos == FOREVER) {
            return false;
        }
        return nowNanos - writtenAtNanos >= ttlNanos;
    }
}
```

**After:**

```java
package net.terminalvalue.crosscut.cache;

/**
 * The expire-after-write time left to a cache entry, with {@code Long.MAX_VALUE} as the time to live meaning "never", as
 * Caffeine and Spring's cache abstraction treat it. The clock reading is passed in, so that the cache can be
 * driven by a {@code Clock} in tests and by {@code System.nanoTime()} in production.
 */
    // ...

    public static final long FOREVER = Long.MAX_VALUE;

    /**
     * How long an entry written at {@code writtenAtNanos} with the given time to live has left at {@code nowNanos},
     * in milliseconds as the cache's metrics report it: zero or
     * negative once it has expired, {@link #FOREVER} for an entry that never does, so that an eviction can be scheduled for
     * when the entry expires and the cache's metrics can report the time left.
     */
    public static long remainingMillis(long writtenAtNanos, long ttlNanos, long nowNanos) {
        if (ttlNanos == FOREVER) {
            return FOREVER;
        }
        return (ttlNanos - (nowNanos - writtenAtNanos)) / 1_000_000L;
    }
}
```

## What the verifier found

The two versions disagree. The prover found this input outside the declared change, and the verifier replayed it in jvmcontract's bytecode interpreter against both versions:

| Input | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `remainingMillis(writtenAtNanos=0, ttlNanos=1, nowNanos=0)` | `false` | `0` |

One disagreeing input is enough to fail the build. The domain is `writtenAtNanos: long × ttlNanos: long × nowNanos: long`; the search tries small values first so that the witness is readable, and would have covered all of it.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

No: every existing unit test passes (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.crosscut.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

An entry in the last fraction of a millisecond of its time to live is reported expired and evicted early. Harmless for a cache on its own, but the same kernel decides whether a cached idempotency record is still live, and an early eviction there lets a retry through as a first request. The four tests pass: they check whole seconds, and a second to go is a thousand milliseconds.

## Why the verdict is right

The relation `previous == (result <= 0)` is compiled into the harness in place of the equality of results, and the proof searches small values first: `remainingMillis(writtenAtNanos=0, ttlNanos=1, nowNanos=0)`, an entry written just now with a nanosecond to live. The previous version says not expired, the time since the write being less than the time to live; the new one returns `1 / 1_000_000`, which is zero, and zero is no time left. The report shows both results and that the relation does not hold between them. The developer's claim was that a millisecond count of zero means expired; the proof shows the count is zero for a whole millisecond before that.

## What to do

Keep the time left in nanoseconds (example 123) and convert where it is reported, or round the milliseconds up, `(remaining + 999_999) / 1_000_000`, so that an entry with any time left reports a millisecond. The module's own property, rewritten for the milliseconds the same way, refutes the change as well.

## Notes

- The library's test of the same shape finds `remainingMillis(writtenAtNanos=0, ttlNanos=1, nowNanos=0)` with JBMC in about a second, before `false` and after `0`, under the line `the results are not related by previous == (result <= 0)`; the measurement on this kernel is the pipeline's.
- The tool's own checker (`--engine native`) finds the same difference in 0.1 s, but on a large input: it has no staged search of small values, and the shrinker's 4000 interpreter runs do not bring three 64-bit values down, so the witness it reports is the raw one. The example runs JBMC.
- The scope excludes the inputs outside the module's precondition (a clock reading from before the write, a non-positive time to live, a write before the clock's zero), as in example 123; the counterexample is well inside it, and is found at the first stage of the search, which tries values up to 20.

## Evidence

How the verdict was reached: found by JBMC 6.11.0 in 0.1 s searching inputs in [0:20] as remainingMillis(writtenAtNanos=0, ttlNanos=16, nowNanos=0), shrunk to the input above in 9 interpreter runs, replayed in the interpreter; domain writtenAtNanos: long × ttlNanos: long × nowNanos: long.

This result was recorded before runs fingerprinted their inputs, so whether it still matches the current patch and sources is not known.

/** Generated by jvmcontract: asserts that two versions of a method agree. The class file JBMC checks is generated directly; this is the same statement, for readers. */
public final class EquivalenceHarness {
    public static void check(long writtenAtNanos, long ttlNanos, long nowNanos) {
        if (!(writtenAtNanos >= 0 && nowNanos >= writtenAtNanos && ttlNanos > 0)) { return; } // the inputs the developer meant to change
        boolean a = false;
        int ea = 0;
        try { a = before.net.terminalvalue.crosscut.cache.Expiry.isExpired(writtenAtNanos, ttlNanos, nowNanos); } catch (java.lang.NumberFormatException t) { ea = 1; } catch (java.lang.ArithmeticException t) { ea = 2; } catch (java.lang.NullPointerException t) { ea = 3; } catch (java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { ea = 4; } catch (java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { ea = 5; } catch (java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException t) { ea = 6; } catch (java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException t) { ea = 7; } catch (java.lang.ClassCastException t) { ea = 8; } catch (java.lang.IllegalStateException t) { ea = 9; } catch (java.lang.IllegalArgumentException t) { ea = 10; } catch (java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException t) { ea = 11; } catch (java.util.NoSuchElementException t) { ea = 12; } catch (java.util.ConcurrentModificationException t) { ea = 13; } catch (java.lang.RuntimeException t) { ea = 14; } catch (java.lang.Error t) { ea = 15; }
        long b = 0;
        int eb = 0;
        try { b = net.terminalvalue.crosscut.cache.Expiry.remainingMillis(writtenAtNanos, ttlNanos, nowNanos); } catch (java.lang.NumberFormatException t) { eb = 1; } catch (java.lang.ArithmeticException t) { eb = 2; } catch (java.lang.NullPointerException t) { eb = 3; } catch (java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { eb = 4; } catch (java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { eb = 5; } catch (java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException t) { eb = 6; } catch (java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException t) { eb = 7; } catch (java.lang.ClassCastException t) { eb = 8; } catch (java.lang.IllegalStateException t) { eb = 9; } catch (java.lang.IllegalArgumentException t) { eb = 10; } catch (java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException t) { eb = 11; } catch (java.util.NoSuchElementException t) { eb = 12; } catch (java.util.ConcurrentModificationException t) { eb = 13; } catch (java.lang.RuntimeException t) { eb = 14; } catch (java.lang.Error t) { eb = 15; }
        // The results agree when the stated relation holds: previous is the previous version's, result the new one's.
        boolean previous = a; long result = b;
        assert ea == eb && (ea != 0 || (previous == (result <= 0)));
    }
}

**Provenance:** Constructed as the millisecond variant of example 123's rewrite, the unit a Spring cache's statistics and `Cache-Control` headers use. The technique is regression verification under a stated relation between the versions' results.

- [Godlin and Strichman, Regression verification: proving the equivalence of similar programs (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1002/stvr.1472)
- [System.nanoTime (Java SE 21): compare two readings by their difference, never by magnitude](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/System.html#nanoTime())
- [Caffeine: expireAfterWrite and the Expiry interface](https://github.com/ben-manes/caffeine/wiki/Eviction#time-based)
